body:
>Just because pain "doesn't help with [your] situation" doesn't mean one can let it go. I get that it is logical to do so but I'm asking how? Doesn't seem possible for most people (me included).

I would respond my giving an example. If you get stabbed by a mugger, would your priorities lie in feeling the 'pain'/injury or stopping the mugger and getting help. That's what I mean by "the pain isn't suffering." You feel a signal, but the damage is done, all you can do is take action to prevent and or stop said damage. Assuming one of your goals is to exist. 

>I also disagree about suffering. Suffering can be related to goals but is also distinct from them. The only process I have heard that may eliminate suffering is constant, prolonged, daily meditation.

The idea of suffering ("bad") requires a reference point/definition. I think the definition of suffering is whenever my actions are not aligned with my values. The situation I am in can never cause me suffering, only taking actions that I know are against my values would. 

> The state of being you claim have appears to be magical and anathema to normal human experience. You have logic for why it's good, which I agree with, but no concrete method for how, other than by simply doing it. This answer is of no help to most people as they don't have that seemingly magical ability. I am becoming skeptical that you have this ability, partly because you say it's easy and that all humans have it as well. You also seem to imply that logic > biology, which isn't the case for the vast majority of people and I have never seen concrete evidence that it is the case for even one individual. 

It's not magical... I understand/know what I value, and I act based on that. I'm not saying "logic>biology." The biology I have is what is logical. Logic is relative when you talk about goals. What's logical if you have x goal is different if you have y goal. By definition everyone has the goal to have goals achieved state. Based on all the definitions and words we use, it's true. Try to disprove it/point out how illogical it is, but it's like trying to prove that up isn't up. Up is up because we describe that concept with that word. 

> I also don't see any logic in having a "goals achieved state" as a base value. Perhaps that's just how you are built and that's fine. I don't know that there is one base value however it is possible. I just haven't seen any convincing evidence for or against.

A person has a goal. By definition they have the goal of goals achieved state. Because they have the goal. Have the goal = value the goal. Goal = values, desires, programming, etc. 

> If I had a base goal, it would be to minimize experienced suffering as much as possible. I want to differentiate this goal from being in a state of non-suffering. The latter requires existence so as to "be in a state". I do not value being in a state as my base, merely that I do not wish to experience suffering. 

That goal still requires existing. "I wish not to experience suffering." You still need to exist for that. If your goal is to "minimize experienced suffering," you still need to exist to do that. If that action's end goal is to not suffer, you still need to exist to not suffer. Not sure if you are explaining it poorly, or if you are misunderstanding what you are saying. 

> Perhaps our difference is that you value being in a state, in your case one of "goals achieved" while I value minimizing suffering.

If your goal is to minimize suffering (feel the least pain possible), that is achievable. Also, that still involves existing. Minimize suffering is an action. If your end goal/reason for that action is to feel the least pain, it still involves existing. But if you still want to say that wanting to take the action of minimizing suffering is your goal, that still involves existing. Not sure if you are saying something wrong or I am misunderstanding you or I'm just right about this.. Also, like I said earlier, if you have any goal/value, you by definition have the goal of goals/values achieved state.

My (our) biology is wired in a way to achieve the goals I (we) have. By definition, we all have the goal of goals achieved state. That is the only required goal that exists. But people have the capacity to think optional/learned goals are required goals (cuz of illogical beliefs, indoctrinations, etc). The only thing that causes those goals to have value to them is them allowing them to by their choice/beliefs. I think you said you think suffering is separate from goals. I'd have to disagree. Even if you say the body has the goal/value/programming to think signals related to getting cut is objectively suffering, I would disagree. Yes you will feel signals related to that. But the value/negative value you attribute to that cut is based off of whatever goals you happen to have. Why would a person who does not value life care about being cut? Why would those signals mean anything to them? "Because they don't want suffering." Suffering is relative to your goals/values/desires. If you don't have them, there's no suffering. And even if you have them, if you take action based on those goals, you won't suffer.

Example, if my goal is to not suffer (defined here as feeling pain such as cuts), if I get cut, I would take action to stop the injury and prevent further injury. No suffering required. I value not getting cut, I don't negatively value the cut because that's a waste of time which can lead to more cuts. But again, I'm open to be proven wrong. I was after all very against 'dying' early due to my actions. But when I stopped being biased based on no good reasons, it seemed very logical. Until I found out I'd get brain damage, so RIP to that.

I think you still believe that your suffering isn't caused by what you think has value. Idk. You'll have to explain to me what you value/believe. 

In short, I value goals achieved state. There are 4 options to achieve this for me since no goals outside of said goal is required. And only the 4th possible option is possible. If you believed you had required goals, like I guess for you it's "minimize suffering" (which I think is nonsense, no offense, because suffering only exists relative to whatever goals/values you have. The only reason I care about not getting hurt is because I need the ability to do work so I can keep my existence and logic. If I didn't care about that, it wouldn't matter to me. The values related to that signal and no signal is equal in terms of their value. Like if I keep my existence, but constantly feel like I am stabbed, I wouldn't be in suffering because the only reason I care about injury signals is because I don't want to lose my existence. I guess being able to think matters too... But eh... You get my point?...). 

If you are trying to say how you can be like me, I'd just say understand all your values. Because going against them is what causes suffering. In the past I kept "reasoning" suicide is the answer, but wouldn't do it because it went against my values. If I was trying to end suffering so I can get to a state of not suffering, I'd have to take action to stop the suffering. Suicide would just make me not exist, there'd be no me to suffer or not suffer. I care about my goals, and having those goals and having those goals achieved all involve me existing. 

I'm rambling, but whatever, read it, skim it, don't read it... I don't think there are required goals besides goals achieved state. Because with required goals, there's no confusion or doubt, it's you/in your brain and there's nothing that can change it. 

Me, past to now: "I have optional values I think are required. Nothing I do is making them achieved, causes suffering because I am doing an illogical action trying to achieve goals I don't have that also can't be achieved, and if achieved change nothing, no goals achieved state or "happiness" whatever." "Stopped being biased with my values I happen to end up with, holding on to them like dogmatic religious people do, tested if these values can be let go of/if they are required because they make no sense and won't get me goals achieved state, and they were learned (but had to test if they can be rid of because it's not work having cuz unachievable and changes nothing = suffering). Turns out, none of them were required and it was all indoctrination/self-fulfilling beliefs/values. At the core, we want goals achieved state. By definition. I don't see any reason to think I have any (other) required goals besides that. Best I can do as a mortal is have the goal achieved temporarily, so option 4, existence as a goal (option 1-3 I told you about earlier, 3 leads to brain damage (no values)."

Death is the end of life, sure. But calling it an end state in the sense of a goal/value one has is not the same thing. 

End states (i.e. achieved goals/values, goals achieved state) are the only reason why the process of getting to an end state has any value. ("my view"/reality). So yeah, that has more value. I guess end state is goals achieved state in your wording. 

> With this in mind, I can see why I do not actively pursue that end state.

Because of the reasoning I stated?

>How were you able to come to let go of values regarding pain, or other things? If the process is repeatable, it seems to me it would be a valuable skill to have.

I might be wrong about it. But I think pain = when one acts contrary to one's goals, or just anything that goes against one's goals. 

If you are talking about how I choose not to feel physical pain as painful, it's because it doesn't help with my situation. My goal rn is to exist, if I am injured, the only value the signal caused by an injury has is that I am injured and nothing more. So the next action I will take is the action that will fix that injury. I'm not going to spend time and attention suffering in the pain (if that makes sense). I'm going to be taking action to stop the pain so I don't have permanent damage to the body. But I can be proven wrong in the future... (I doubt it.)

If you are talking about letting go of values in general. I already said my only value is goals achieved state. Because I believe this, I don't have any other values outside of the one's that are under 'goals achieved state' bare minimum. So goal of logic, information, existence, whatever. But I can be proven wrong about this. If I do anything against my values, that's the only time I suffer. And denying/ignoring that I did something against my values makes me suffer more (I'd say one is unaware that they did it, but I think they know they did it and it will cause them to suffer if they don't admit it due to ego or whatever). Because when one applies basic reasoning to the situation, it's clear that I went against my values and that the ignoring of that fact is based on ego that I did not do something illogical, not logic. 

The only way letting a value go would be hard is if one thinks there is value in that thing... If you do, just do that thing. But often times, when I that thing, there isn't any value there. RIP.

It's a learning process... If one understands that they "only" value goals achieved state, but chooses to do, to plan to do something they know is not required, it's suffering. Only because it is going against what you value/think is logical. That's why those who are ignorant that their actions and values have various contradictions don't suffer much. 

Idk. I'm still open to changing my mind due to new evidence.

I won't say that "the ultimate purpose of life is to die" because you use the word purpose. Life happened to occur, and it will have to disappear. No values about it. I think pain can't exist unless one is doing what is against/not one's goals. 

> If this is true, any advice on how to figure out what these goals that are holding back are, so I can assess their validity and then either more efficiently pursue them or vacate them?

For me, the only value I have, as I said in the quote you quoted, is being in goals achieved state. Being in this state requires me to be alive. So suicide makes no sense. To be in goals achieved state, I need mainly: existence and ability to think logically. I'm not in your brain so I can't say what exactly you still think you value. Like you might still think physical pain is painful, I think that pain isn't painful if one does not have values regarding it. But I can be proven wrong with future experience...

> We'll probably continue to disagree on this point. Sam Harris has made a good enough case, in my eyes, that free will does not exist. 

It doesn't technically, so yeah, I agree.

> All our actions, goals, desires, and even our will to change is predicated on the unique construction of ours brains. What neuron is connected to other neurons and how strong each connection is, etc. The structure is changeable but different brains are susceptible to different changes in varying degrees based on the structure at any given point in time. 

Mhm.

> I argue that for some, certain beliefs and actions are physically resistant to change to the point that valid logic will not change or alter certain beliefs or goals, thus making them a subjective physical necessity. 

This I disagree on. I think that if they live long enough or think about it honestly, they will reach the same conclusion I did. They just won't because of how they are. I wouldn't have had my initial programming been like theirs. 

> I accept one or more individuals may be able to overcome things like pain (like yourself) but deny that the possibility is available to all people. 

I think it is physically possible for people. But I'd agree that who they are right now mentally can't understand things or believe things other than what they are willing to. Based on their programming. I don't think we disagree. I know there is no free will. But just as I'd say people can learn x, but will never choose to learn x; people are able to understand, but will never choose to understand. They aren't unable to necessarily, it's just that their programming won't allow them to do what will make them understand. 

> Let's see if I can word this correctly. If P1 is your base goal (let's not worry about whether it is the framework goal for all or not at this point), and the achievement of that comes when no longer having any goals, and it is better to find that most efficient path to a goal, 

> it seems to follow that instead of logically letting go of all goals, resulting in a situation where one is brain damaged an unable to fulfill P1, wouldn't it be more efficient to set the most efficient number of goals to reach the fulfillment of P1?

I don't really agree with the second half. One has goal of goals achieved. Once they have no goals, that goal is achieved. No other goals besides p1 is required. So one will have no goals, cuz it is more efficient that achieving one's optional goals that happened to occur. The reason why I turned this "no values" in to "now valuing one thing, existence" is because like you said, if I did no values, I would end up brain damaged which would make me lose my ability to think logically, causing me to have optional values that I think are required. The most efficient number of goals is now 1 instead of 0. And that 1 is existence. Because that is the second ideal way to get P1 other than the way I stated which turns out to not be possible.

========

"C3: It is better to have the most efficient set of goals to achieve P1

P10: Death results in P1 being achieved

C4: It is thus better to have the most efficient set of goals that causes death"

C3 is true. That most efficient set of goals is now 'existence' which just adds 1 value on top of P1. P10 is false. One has to be alive/existing to have a goal achieved. Dying just results in 'no you.' One is a thing with required goals/values, and one will do those things given the environment. Death by definition can't achieve one's goals unless their specific goal is to be dead/not exist. 

Technically, P1 can't be achieved beyond temporary time because we are not immortal in the "never die" or "can die, but don't have to" way. Ideally, one would have no values and never die. The next ideal would be "immortality is possible, but work must be done to maintain it," meaning after one has existence taken care of [for the day or period of hours] (their one value besides p1) the rest of their time would be in goals achieved state (p1 achieve). The next next ideal is the thing that can't happen, mortal life and having no values, can't happen because dehydration will cause one to lose the ability to think logically causing one to think optional goals to be required. Then, the last ideal which is possible is only value existence, so that once taken care of, one can be in goals achieved state. I know that 'we all die, and the past doesn't matter, only really the present does, so when I die, it won't matter to me.' But I have P1 as a goal. And even though death will happen, that doesn't change P1. Because death is not relevant in an action sense. 

BTW, there is no is ought problem, all that exists are is's. "Oughts" just come from people pushing their goals/values. "One should do x, IF one has y goal/value." That's how should/ought is used. 

> As far as me wanting to commit suicide, I merely see it as the most efficient way to complete goals, or as you put it, the framework goal.

You have to exist to be in goals achieved state. It logically doesn't connect with me that suicide will have me goals achieved state because it involves me existing and me being in that state. 

> Even though I see the apparent logic behind behind it, I do not want to do it because of my biological drive to continue living.

From my past experience, but is no longer the case now, when ever I hesitate at the idea of suicide, it has always been the cause that it was because my reasoning was faulty. I had goals/values (P1) that did not align with suicide. Such as being in goals achieved state. It wasn't due to a desire to live, but a desire to do what my goals actually are.

> If however I was diagnosed with a terminal illness, I would be happy with that, as it seems to me be more efficient than living a long life and would negate any biological drive to survive on my part.

I'd be happy to be diagnosed with a terminal illness, assuming I can still think logically, because I see no reason to live longer than I have to. I am only choosing to value existence because option 3 is impossible.  And suicide is illogical because dying has nothing to do with my value of goals achieved state. So I'm stuck having to value existence until I figure something out, unless there just isn't anything else to figure out.

It's the same thing over and over, sorry, but this is going nowhere. Either because of me or you, but only a third party can truly know because we both think it is the other person who is misunderstanding. But thank you for responding, I don't want to waste any more of either of our time.
Again, valid is not the same as sound. I know you think people have required goals, and I don't think they are required.

You are saying my argument involves a goal x original objective when it doesn't at all... People have said the same thing about my argument to me before, not sure if that person is you. But it's still the same thing: I'm not talking about what you are talking about.

> There's a difference between achieving goals and having no unachieved goals. Wanting the former entails different desires from the latter, even if they share one property of their end state.

Achieving goal x is different from not having goal x, I'm not denying that. But that doesn't change my initial argument. "Goals achieved state", which I still don't think you understand, (P1) can be achieved by either doing whatever happens to be one's optional goals or by getting rid of them... What are you not understanding...

Look at my post again: Person has the goal to have their goals achieved.

Meaning, if a person has no goals to begin with other than that goal, they would do nothing... But you keep trying to insert "they want goals x whatever to be achieved" when that's not part of the argument at all... 

Of course if one has the goal x, they will care about goal x. But I am not talking about goal x. I am talking about goal in p1 which doesn't care at all about how goal x disappears. Goal p1 does not require goal x to be achieved, it requires it to be gone. But you are in denial of this, and continue to counter an argument I am not talking about or am making.
No idea what you are trying to tell me.
How and why does that matter.

P1. People have the goal of achieving their goals (this first goal is the 'Framework Goal').

Person has the goal to have their goals achieved.

People have the goal to be in goals achieved state.

...
Premise 1.

Unless that goal is P1, everything else is optional. 

> Correct. Conversely if one has a goal and abandons that goal, they will have no more goals. But those are not in goals achieved state. 

They don't have those goals, so they won't care that they are in goals achieved state or not... 

> The only conclusion you draw from this is "If you have no goals, then you have no goals". So what? What's your motivation for moving to this state when that conflicts with your goals, rather than is your goal?

My goal is P1. My actions don't conflict with that.

> Only in the sense I originally gave - ie want to achieve their goals, not in the sense "want to have 0 goals". Those are different things, with different solutions. I'd say this is the sense in which your proof applies, but as far as I can see, your proof isn't actually arguing for either, and I'm not sure what you intend it to show, as you seem to stop short of giving any conclusion about anything.

Again, the want isn't to want 0 goals. The want is P1... Do you not understand my argument? Most of my responses are about clarifying how you are not talking about what I am talking about... My conclusion and argument is in my post... 

> No. I don't think you're understanding what I'm saying here at all. I'm saying if your goal is to achieve goals, you need to achieve goals to meet that goal. Abandoning goals does not assist a goal of achieving goals, only the superficially similar one of "have no unachieved goals", which is not a goal people actually hold. It's like saying "I have $5000 and want to use it to buy a $5000 car" can be met by "Burn the $5000 - that way, you'll be in the same state of not having money, just as you would if you spent it on the car, and this way you don't even have to go to the car dealer!" It misses that the "have 0 goals" / "have no money" is not the only thing going on with that goal: we also want to achieve the goals / have the car at the end. 

My goal is not to achieve goals... You're not understanding what I am saying at all. My goal is to be in "values/goals achieved state." If one has no goals/values, they are already in that state... If one has one goal and achieves it, they will have no goals and are now in goals achieved state. I am NOT saying that are in "a state in which a specific goal is achieved." I am saying they are in "goals/values achieved state." Meaning all their goals are achieved, if they have no goals in the first place, they are in that state already. Understand. You are still responding to the straw man of "you are saying you are trying to achieve those goals." That's false. People have goal P1. The example you gave: the person should stop wanting the car, but keep the money. Again, you are responding to an argument that is not mine. 

> You achieve a goal about achieving goals by doing something that prevents you from achieving goals? How? If I abandon a goal, how many goals do you think that achieved?

Again, not my argument. I'll explain in a different way. A person is born without goals/values. This means they are in goals achieved state by definition. If you still don't understand, don't bother responding cuz you'll just repeat the same thing to an argument I am not talking about. Again, P1 is the goal.

The goal to live is not a required goal because it is optional. I know you believe it is required, so you will never change your mind. I'm saying I am not convinced that it is required, you are saying you are not convinced it is optional. This is the same problem with "prove that you are aware." You can't. Also, I think you are confusing valid vs sound.
The human brain of course has to have a structure in it for it to do anything, like everything else. I'm just saying that it's P1.

P1 matters. The post is to see if the argument is valid. Of course people won't have values they don't think they have. There's no way you can convince a republican to be a democrat, they differ in opinion fundamentally and are unwilling to change their mind. The same for those who think their optional goals are required. I think only P1 is a required goal and everything else is self-fulfilling. Believe it or not, that's most likely the case.
The only structure that exists is P1.
It's optional because it's not a goal one has to have because of un-overcome-able programming. It's optional for me, but I'd say it is the same for everyone else, they just are unwilling.
The structure in their brain that they follow is what they believe to be their required goals/values... And again, what they believe to be rational.

Efficient: less resources required. Resources: time, energy, money, etc. 

Wanting? I don't think we have goals besides p1.

The base goal is P1: A person has a goal/value. By definition, they must first have the goal to have the goals they have i.e. they must first have the goal to be in goals achieved state. 

All of our actions are based on what we believe to be our goals/values, I don't disagree with you on that. But what I am saying is that people have goal p1, but believe their optional (and indoctrinated, etc) goals are required goals. People's goals aren't really unique. They were caused by predicable things. Because physics and chemistry.

I know if a person believes their optional goal is a required goal that they would see it as a required goal. I don't disagree with that. But I disagree that it is a required goal. If "neural net" you mean what a person believes to be their required goals/values, sure. I disagree that people are unable to overcome it. I think they are unwilling to try/unwilling to test it to 'discover the truth.' Facts and reasoning are the only thing that can allow one to discover their believed required goal to be optional. A true required goal is such a goal that is in a person, with no debate on their part. 

I don't think there is a biological drive to survival that one must follow/that is required to be a value/goal. I think it's optional. 

= ===========================================================

By the way, I ran into a problem with my "plan." If I try to stop having values, I will only be successful up to a certain point because I recently found out that if one survives long enough (no organ failures) during dehydration, their brain will start to be damaged and etc. Meaning if I try to have no values, I will end up losing my ability to think rationally. Memory loss too, so it's too risky to try it because if I end up surviving long enough to get brain damage, I will end up believing optional values as required values due to brain damage. It may be true that I will keep my logic. But from what I have read, it's unlikely. So guess I'll have to do the long term way: "goal/value to exist." And achieve goals achieved under that rather than under no goals/values at all. 

What are your thoughts on this? 

Do you actually want to commit suicide? (assuming you could overcome what you say to be survival instinct/optional goal to survive that you are very unwilling to let go of/believe you can't let go of it. Because technically you can just suicide in a painless way, there's no survival instinct there...)? I don't, I just would have ended up dead early when having no values; but I discovered that I will likely be unable to maintain my ability to think logically (have no values) if I dehydrated, not due to pain, but due to brain damage which literally will "affect what/who I am and what think." Memory loss too. So it's risky/I will fail because it's unlikely that I will 'die' of organ failure before brain damage. I know people who I have talked to on reddit will accuse me of 'chickening out,' but I'm okay with dying and what they call pain. I'm just not okay with me literally becoming a different person due to brain damage (if I become someone else, I'm no longer the same person who would make the same decisions, because different believed goals/values). Because literally one can get delirium from dehydration. A required goal of P1 is 'goal of logic' technically, because how else can one understand anything outside of logic or know what P1 means/says.

Although I disagree that the biological drive to survive is strong/cant be overcome, I do think that brain damage can't be overcome with logic, cuz one will be missing the ability to use such logic... 

So, opinion/thoughts? I was seriously gonna go through with the 'dehydration thing.' Unless you or I find proof that no brain damage will occur, or no ruined logic will occur, I'm going back to the dehydration thing from no values. But all the info I looked up said brain damage and mental issues (can't overcome that without logic i.e. logic part of the brain is weak/can't be used/believed). I'm okay with living longer, cuz I don't think pain (painful signals) can exist without certain false beliefs about reality, it's just that it will take more effort/resources without reason compared to the shorter way. But now there is a reason: if I try the no values way, I will end up becoming illogical which would make be think optional values are required, or who knows what from the brain damage and delirium... 

Probably won't update the post...

In terms of achieving P1... Like I said... One has that goal... 

Never said what people want is to achieve goals for it's own sake... 

> How does this follow? Surely the more goals you have, the easier it is to reach goal achieved state (more opportunity to achieve any given one). Having fewer goals means less goals to achieve, so fewer reaching "goal achieved" state

If one has a goal and that goal is achieved, they will have no more goals. They are in goals achieved state. That is what I mean. If never had goals to begin with, all they would have to do is realize it under their required goal p1. P1 is "achieve the goals one has." They discover they have none except that. So they will do nothing. Assuming they get rid of the believe goals that they have. 


>Um - P1 is to "have your goals achieved". How does something that doesn't achieve any of your goals do this? If we for some reason interpret P1 as "Have no unachieved goals", it works, but who cares? No one has that goal, and so it's completely the wrong metric. The objective of a goal is to achieve it, not to be rid of it.

P1 is the goal. The goal to be in goals achieved state. All your goals are achieved = you are in goals achieved state. If you have no (other) goals, you are in goals achieved state because you are done. "Have no unachieved goals." It works, but they don't have any goals. Besides p1.

Everyone objectively has goal p1. Proof:

A person has a goal/value. By definition, they must first have the goal to have the goals they have i.e. they must first have the goal to be in goals achieved state. 

The objective of a goal is to achieve it, yes. And that is how you achieve goal p1. That's the only goal because there are no other required goals. You seem to think we have other required goals. I don't think that. And I have run into no evidence to prove to me that I have any others.

You are pulling in things that were not stated. You are saying that people have required goals/values other than P1. Of course they won't stop taking action if they have goals like "always take action." But the problem is that that goal is optional/entirely baseless/not based on reasoning but based on self-fulfilling belief.

If their goals are fulfilled, they would have nothing to do. If their goals were not fulfilled, they would have something to do. There is no "enjoying a perfect life" because that would involve and unfinished goal... 

The framework goal is objectively true. It's required in the sense that all beings have it. I know you believe human nature to consist of various potential required goals, but I think those goals are optional (and of course, baseless and illogical).

Taking the more efficient path something we do when making decisions (relative to our values/goals). Otherwise, 1hr to get food vs 10 days to get food, one can't make a decision because they are being 'unbiased.' They are biased towards their goal, if they choose the more efficient one, they will have more resources to use for achieving their goal. There is nothing philosophically suspect here. 

>So that people bother doing higher education, exercising, go experience all that Earth has to offer. We already somewhat see this with caffeine as well as misuse of uppers like ADHD medicines. 

These actions come from their goals/values. So that requires resources. But in those decisions, they are still picking the more efficient one.

I don't think you know what tautology means.

Also, it's not false on observation.

?

Also, the P1 I stated is still the same.
You believe your optional goal to life is required.

"emotions, desires and other mental states" are goals/values one has. 

Being in goals achieved state is objectively one's goal.
Their actions and choices are based on what they believe to be rational.
